qGfoYja1|nKo`SgoBFN4.text:
made by @Patcail

Hello! So you want to use this machine, huh? You've came to the right place! This engine can store numbers up to f_w+1 (1000) This engine can represent Graham's number quite cleanly: [Infinity]^63 [3][2][1][1]1.11. Negative numbers have partial support. 

To understand how it works, it's a good idea to go here: 

https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/337265163/

and learn how to use OmegaNum. That's because this engine is simply an extension of OmegaNum.

Assuming you know how OmegaNum works, the way this works is by adding a new bracket number: [Infinity]. The way [Infinity] works is very simple.

[Infinity]n=[3]n if n<=2
[infinity]n=[n]10 otherwise.

We will also define decimal index like this:
[n]10=[floor(n)+1]2*5^mod(n,1)

This makes [infinity]x acts like Jx, and Graham's number is J^63 GFEE1.11

New Examples:
You may have infinity arrows. In this case, a^^...^^b with infinity arrows becomes
a^^...^^a with b arrows!
However, it does not support encoded third entries, so you can't do 3^^...^^5 with [1]7 arrows, or Arrows(3, 5, [1]7)







You can also take the infini-logarithm too! It counts the number of arrows!











Here, I made a script that accurately calculates Graham's number! You should get J^63 GF7.62e12
























There's no need to stop there. We can calculate g_1000 if we want to. The limit is g_200000, because that's the limit of list size.


Note: If you want to upgrade from OmegaNum to ExpantaNum, you simply need to replace these blocks
